intro: A padded batch costs its longest sequence length times its row count. Packing by the sum of raw lengths can underestimate memory and overflow a token budget.
task: Pack sequences by padded computation cost while preserving input order and respecting both token and row budgets.
requirements: lengths is a vector of positive integer-valued sequence lengths, possibly empty. token_budget and max_batch_size are integers 1..1000000; every length must fit the token budget alone.
Process sequences in original order. Append a sequence to the current batch only when new_max_length*new_count<=token_budget and new_count<=max_batch_size; otherwise start a new batch.
Return dict batches as lists of original indices and padded_tokens as one integer cost per batch. Do not reorder, split, or discard sequences.

Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, except where a stricter bound is stated. Booleans are not numeric parameters. Leave all caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Recompute the tentative maximum
hints.body: Adding one long sequence can increase the padding cost for every row already in the batch.

hints.title: Flush before adding an oversized combination
hints.body: The current batch stays valid; the incoming sequence begins the next batch.

explanation: Dense padded computation often scales with batch_size times max_length, not the sum of true sequence lengths. The batch planner must account for this shared padding cost.
This lesson uses an order-preserving greedy policy rather than sorting or optimizing globally. Keeping original order makes the output predictable and preserves a caller-defined sequence schedule.
